arp_spoofing.pcap.story: An unknown device keeps telling one PC that it is the router, and telling the router that it is that PC, so the PC's traffic flows through the intruder.
arp_spoofing.pcap.title: ARP spoofing of the router (man-in-the-middle)

busy_but_healthy.pcap.story: A busy afternoon with thousands of healthy flows, including harmless oddities like a lone retransmission, a typo'd domain and a traceroute.
busy_but_healthy.pcap.title: Busy but healthy

clean_office.pcap.story: An ordinary office: a laptop joins by DHCP, people browse, mail and docs sync, nothing is wrong.
clean_office.pcap.title: Clean office afternoon

cleartext_creds.pcap.story: An admin logs in to the NAS over FTP, to the router over Telnet and to the printer's admin page over plain HTTP: anyone on the network could read those passwords.
cleartext_creds.pcap.title: Passwords sent in plain text

connection_refused.pcap.story: An application server keeps connecting to a database at 192.168.1.20:5432 whose service is stopped, so every attempt is refused with a reset.
connection_refused.pcap.title: Database connection refused

dhcp_misconfig_two_routers.pcap.story: Someone plugged a home router into the office LAN with DHCP enabled; clients now receive two offers and the ones that take the 192.168.0.x lease lose internet and DNS.
dhcp_misconfig_two_routers.pcap.title: Second DHCP server from a home router

dhcp_no_server.pcap.story: The DHCP server is down: laptops broadcast DISCOVERs with growing backoff, get no offer, and fall back to 169.254.x.x link-local addresses.
dhcp_no_server.pcap.title: No DHCP server

dns_failure.pcap.story: The office DNS resolver at 192.168.1.1 stops responding: lookups time out and are retried, some fail with SERVFAIL, and a few only answer after seconds, so web pages hang.
dns_failure.pcap.title: Resolver stops answering

dns_hijack.pcap.story: Whenever someone looks up the bank's login site, a forged answer pointing to a device inside the office arrives before the real one, so people are silently sent to the intruder.
dns_hijack.pcap.title: DNS hijacking: forged answers for the bank

dns_tunnel.pcap.story: One PC sends hundreds of lookups for long random-looking names under one domain, at a steady rhythm: the typical sign of malware smuggling data out through DNS.
dns_tunnel.pcap.title: Data hidden inside DNS lookups (DNS tunnelling)

high_latency.pcap.story: Every connection takes 600 to 900 ms just to complete its handshake because the uplink is a very high-latency satellite path; the servers themselves answer quickly.
high_latency.pcap.title: Satellite-grade latency

host_sweep.pcap.story: An unknown device asks for every address from .1 to .254, pings each device that answers, then checks which ones have Windows file sharing (port 445) open.
host_sweep.pcap.title: Network sweep: mapping every device

ip_conflict.pcap.story: A printer with a static address and a guest laptop configured by hand both use 192.168.1.23; both answer ARP for it and both send their own normal traffic, so connections to either are unreliable.
ip_conflict.pcap.title: Two devices share 192.168.1.23

lossy_link.pcap.story: A laptop on a flaky Wi-Fi link downloads a large file and loses 5 to 8 percent of the segments in both directions, so TCP keeps retransmitting.
lossy_link.pcap.title: Lossy Wi-Fi link

malformed/bad_magic.pcap.story: 4 KiB of random bytes with a .pcap name.
malformed/bad_magic.pcap.title: Not a capture

malformed/compressed_padding.pcap.gz.story: A tiny gzip that expands to a valid pcap header followed by 50 MB of zero bytes; the reader must stop at its decompression cap.
malformed/compressed_padding.pcap.gz.title: Decompression bomb-ish

malformed/corrupt_packets.pcap.story: A well-formed pcap whose frames have broken headers: bad IHL, TCP data offset past the end, a DNS compression pointer loop, a DHCP option running off the end, a truncated ARP and random garbage.
malformed/corrupt_packets.pcap.title: Corrupt packets inside a valid file

malformed/huge_caplen.pcap.story: A record header that claims a 2 GiB packet; the reader must not try to allocate it.
malformed/huge_caplen.pcap.title: Absurd record length

malformed/truncated.pcap.story: A valid capture that was cut off in the middle of its last record (for example a crashed sniffer).
malformed/truncated.pcap.title: Truncated capture

mitm_chain.pcap.story: A rogue DHCP server makes a laptop use it as router and DNS server, then answers the bank's name with its own address and collects the password sent over plain HTTP.
mitm_chain.pcap.title: Man-in-the-middle chain: rogue DHCP → fake DNS → stolen login

mtu_blackhole.pcap.story: A VPN path silently drops every full-size 1460-byte packet and sends no ICMP, so small packets flow but the server's big data segments are retransmitted again and again and the connection stalls.
mtu_blackhole.pcap.title: Path MTU black hole

mtu_frag_needed.pcap.story: The office router tells a laptop that its 1460-byte packets do not fit the 1400-byte VPN tunnel (ICMP fragmentation needed), after which the laptop sends smaller packets.
mtu_frag_needed.pcap.title: Fragmentation needed on a VPN path

outage_vs_attack_mixed.pcap.story: The DNS server stops answering (a genuine fault) while, unrelated, an unknown device scans the file server (an attack): two different problems that look like one to users.
outage_vs_attack_mixed.pcap.title: An outage and an attack at the same time

pcapng_office.pcapng.story: A short healthy office capture saved in pcapng format.
pcapng_office.pcapng.title: Clean office (pcapng)

port_scan.pcap.story: An unknown device quickly knocks on 1,024 ports of the office file server (plus stealth FIN/NULL/Xmas and UDP probes) to find which services are open.
port_scan.pcap.title: Port scan against the file server

rogue_dhcp.pcap.story: An unknown device answers address requests faster than the real router and hands out itself as the router and DNS server, so new laptops send all their traffic through it.
rogue_dhcp.pcap.title: Rogue DHCP server

routing_loop.pcap.story: Packets to 198.51.100.99 bounce between the office router and a second router until their TTL runs out, so the same packet is seen over and over and the sender gets ICMP time exceeded.
routing_loop.pcap.title: Routing loop between two routers

server_down_timeouts.pcap.story: A web service at 198.51.100.7 is down so connection attempts time out with exponential backoff, and the office printer at 192.168.1.50 no longer answers ARP.
server_down_timeouts.pcap.title: Server down, printer unplugged

slow_server.pcap.story: The network is fine (25 ms handshakes) but the API server takes 2 to 6 seconds to send the first byte of every response.
slow_server.pcap.title: Slow application server

syn_flood.pcap.story: Thousands of connection requests per second from random, spoofed internet addresses overwhelm the intranet web server, so real staff can't open it.
syn_flood.pcap.title: SYN flood against the intranet server

tls_failures.pcap.story: Every attempt to open the legacy intranet site is aborted by the browser because the site's certificate has expired.
tls_failures.pcap.title: Secure connections failing: expired certificate

web_bruteforce.pcap.story: One device tries to log in to the intranet 45 times in a row and is refused every time: a password-guessing attack.
web_bruteforce.pcap.title: Password guessing against the intranet login

xss_payload.pcap.story: Normal traffic, except that names inside DNS, DHCP, HTTP and TLS packets contain HTML/JavaScript; reports must show them as plain text and never run them.
xss_payload.pcap.title: Hostile text inside packets (XSS test)

zero_window.pcap.story: A slow laptop downloading an update keeps running out of receive buffer, advertising a zero window and stalling the transfer for seconds at a time.
zero_window.pcap.title: Receiver stalls (zero window)
